results.summary: This project is an 8-bit R2R digital-to-analog converter that is a duplicate of Matt Venn's design. It accepts eight digital input bits and produces an analog output voltage on one analog pin, with an external data input and a load divider control. Testing involves setting the external data input high, driving the eight inputs, and measuring the analog output with a multimeter. The documentation is minimal and refers to the original project for details, so the design's specifics are not fully described here.

This design implements a neural network accelerator for MNIST handwriting prediction in Verilog. It uses a 4x2 tile area and runs at 10 MHz, with all pins labeled generically as ui, uio, and uo. The documentation is essentially absent, providing only the title and one-line description, so no details on architecture, usage, or testing are available. The project is notable for targeting a neural network ASIC but lacks sufficient documentation to verify its functionality.

This is a voltage-controlled LC oscillator designed for 2 GHz operation in Skywater 130nm. It has four analog pins: differential outputs vout_p and vout_n, a control voltage input vctrl, and a bias current input ibias. The documentation is minimal, consisting only of the title and pin names, with no description of how it works or how to test it. External hardware such as a bias current source and control voltage source would be needed to operate it.

This Verilog design generates a VGA demo that displays a virtual 7-segment LED display with decimal point, controlled by 8-bit input. It also has a demo mode that counts down from 9 to 0 and toggles the decimal bit, but the reset for this mode is flawed. The design requires a TinyVGA PMOD for output and runs at 25.175 MHz. Silicon tests confirm the basic display and user input work, but the demo mode does not reset correctly.

This design plays the Nyan Cat animation and music on infinite repeat. It outputs VGA video signals and a PWM audio signal, requiring a TinyVGA PMOD and Mike's audio PMOD for full functionality. The design runs at 25 MHz and has been tested successfully on silicon, with testers reporting that it delighted children. It is a simple, self-contained demo with no inputs.

This Verilog design outputs a waggling 6-bit rainbow demo on VGA, with effects controlled by input pins. Inputs enable dual mode (horizontal flip per scanline) and horizontal waves, with offsets controlling wave speeds. It requires a TinyVGA PMOD and runs at 25.175 MHz. The design can be tested in a VGA playground or with hardware, and an incomplete cocotb testbench is provided.

This chip performs cross- or auto-correlation on PDM microphone inputs to find time difference of arrival or pitch. It uses shift registers and XOR summation, with a decimator and SPI-configurable settings. It outputs PCM audio via I2S and requires external microphones, a clock generator, and an SPI port. The design is notable for its customizable correlation and beamforming capabilities.

This design filters a specific pitch and its harmonics from PDM microphone input using a variable decimator and moving average filter. The filter length is set to samplerate divided by target frequency, and settings are configurable via SPI. It outputs PCM audio over I2S and requires a digital PDM microphone, SPI controller, and I2S receiver. The project is notable for its customizable pitch filtering in the PDM domain.

This Verilog design displays a parody of the 'graphic design is my passion' meme with bouncing shapes on a VGA monitor. It has no inputs and outputs standard VGA signals, requiring a TinyVGA PMOD. The design runs at 25.175 MHz and has been tested successfully on silicon. It is a simple graphics demo with no interactive elements.

This SystemVerilog design generates a random number from 0 to F when a button is pressed, using an inverter ring as the entropy source. It outputs the result on 8 output pins, intended for a 2-digit LED display. The design runs at 50 MHz and requires external hardware for the button and display. The documentation is sparse, with pin names all labeled '1', but the basic function is clear.
